title: Maximum 69 Number
description: Brute force to optimized: trying every flip versus a single greedy left to right pass, then a pure arithmetic version with no extra space.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given a positive number whose digits are only 6s and 9s, change at most one digit, and only from 6 to 9, to make the number as large as possible.

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Detail"],"rows":[["Pattern","Greedy choice driven by place value: the most significant digit that can be improved should always be the one that gets changed."],["Difficulty","Beginner"],["Tags","Math, Greedy"],["Interview Focus","Recognizing that only the leftmost 6 ever matters, then dropping the extra O(d) space used by a digit array in favor of pure place value arithmetic."]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

You are given a positive number num whose digits are only 6s and 9s. You may change at most one digit, and only a 6 can become a 9 (never the other way around). Return the largest number you can produce.

blocks.title: Analogy: The Scoreboard With Two Flip Panels
blocks.text: Picture an old mechanical scoreboard where every digit is a flip panel that can only show a 6 or a 9. You are allowed exactly one flip, from 6 to 9. The panel furthest to the left is worth the most, the same way the thousands digit matters more than the ones digit. So the single best move is always to flip the leftmost panel that currently shows a 6, since that gives the biggest possible jump in value.

blocks.caption: The one rule that solves this problem

blocks.text: There is only one 6 to flip, giving 9999.
Example: num = 9999

There is no 6 anywhere in this number, so nothing can be changed. The answer is simply the number itself: 9999. This is the edge case worth checking directly, since the change is optional, not required.
5. How Should We Think?
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about what actually decides the best move here.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Every digit position has a fixed place value, and a digit further to the left always represents a bigger place value than one to its right.

Observation 2: Only one flip is allowed, from 6 to 9, so the real question is which single 6, if any, gives the biggest possible increase.

Observation 3: Flipping any 6 always adds the exact same amount, 3 times that digit's place value, since 9 minus 6 is always 3.

Observation 4: Since place value only depends on position, the flip with the biggest place value, the leftmost 6, always wins or ties. There is never a reason to consider any other 6.
That reasoning alone already rules out trying every 6, only the leftmost one is ever worth touching.
6. Brute Force Solution
The most literal way to solve this is to try flipping every single 6 one at a time, build the resulting number for each attempt, and keep whichever one turned out largest.
Step by step algorithm

items: Break num into its individual digits.
For every digit that is a 6, build a full candidate number with just that one 6 flipped to a 9.
Convert each candidate back into a number and compare it against the best one seen so far.
Return the largest candidate found (or num itself, if it had no 6 at all).

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: try flipping every 6, keep the best result

codes.python:
def maximum69_number(num):
    digits = list(str(num))          # break the number into individual characters
    best = num                       # start with no change as a valid candidate
    for i in range(len(digits)):
        if digits[i] == '6':          # try flipping this particular 6
            candidate = digits.copy()  # work on a fresh copy so other 6s stay untouched
            candidate[i] = '9'
            best = max(best, int(''.join(candidate)))  # rebuild the number and compare
    return best                       # the largest candidate seen, or num itself if no 6 existed


if __name__ == "__main__":
    num = 9669
    print(maximum69_number(num))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A fresh copy of the digit list is made for every candidate flip, specifically so flipping one 6 never accidentally affects any other 6 still being considered.
best starts at num itself, not 0, since the problem explicitly allows leaving the number completely unchanged when it contains no 6.
Candidates are compared as integers, not as text, avoiding subtle bugs from comparing numbers of different lengths as strings.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
This works because it never guesses, it tries every legal single-flip move and directly compares the results, so the true maximum is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(d squared), where d is the number of digits. Up to d different 6s can be flipped, and rebuilding a candidate number costs O(d) each time.
Space: O(d) for the digit list and whichever candidate is currently being built.

Limitation: trying every 6 is unnecessary work. Because a digit further to the left always represents a bigger place value, flipping the leftmost 6 always produces a result at least as large as flipping any 6 to its right. There is no case where checking the other 6s changes the answer.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every 6 is unnecessary: a digit further left always has a bigger place value than one further right, so no 6 to the right of the leftmost one can ever produce a bigger result.

What it wastes: the brute force rebuilds and compares up to d full candidate numbers, when d minus 1 of those comparisons can never actually win.

Can the search stop early: yes, the very first 6 encountered while scanning left to right is guaranteed to be the best possible flip.

Do we still need to try every digit after that: no, once the leftmost 6 is flipped, nothing left to the right can beat it, so the scan can stop immediately.

The core idea: scan left to right, flip the first 6 found, stop immediately.

Since the leftmost 6 always gives the best (or tied for best) result, the search does not need to consider every 6 at all. The optimization is to scan digits from left to right and stop the very first time a 6 is found.
This turns a problem that was trying d different candidates into a problem that only ever builds one candidate.
9. Optimized Solution
Scan the digits from left to right. The moment a 6 shows up, flip it to a 9 and stop scanning immediately, there is nothing left to gain by continuing.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: stop at the first 6 found

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because place value strictly decreases moving right, so the leftmost 6 always represents the largest possible gain available. Once it is flipped, every remaining digit, 6 or 9, is guaranteed to represent a smaller place value, so continuing the scan could never improve the result, only waste time confirming what is already known.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["No 6 anywhere in num","The loop finishes without ever flipping anything","num is returned unchanged"],["At least one 6 present","The loop flips the first 6 it encounters, the leftmost and most significant one, then stops","The largest possible single-flip result"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The scan explicitly moves left to right, index 0 upward, matching the order digits are stored in the string, which is also most significant to least significant.
break is used the instant a 6 is flipped, specifically because continuing the scan cannot possibly improve the answer, only waste time.
Rebuilding the number from the digit array at the end works correctly whether or not any flip actually happened.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(d), one left to right pass over the digits at most.
Space: O(d) for the digit array built from the number.
10. Further Optimization (If Possible)

The optimized solution still allocates a digit array (or string) of length d just to scan it once. That allocation can be skipped entirely by working with place values directly on the integer, using only division and multiplication by powers of 10.

Intuition: the place value of the leading digit can be found by repeatedly dividing by 10 until nothing is left. From there, checking each digit from the most significant place down to the ones place just needs one division and one modulo, no array required. The moment a 6 is found, adding 3 times that place value (since 9 minus 6 is 3) produces the flipped number directly.
Dry run for num = 9669

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Place value","Digit at this place","Action","Why"],"rows":[["1","1000","9","Not a 6, move to the next place value","Only a 6 can be flipped, so a 9 is simply skipped and the next smaller place value is checked."],["2","100","6","Found it, return 9669 plus 3 times 100","Adding 3 times this place value is mathematically identical to changing this one digit from 6 to 9."]]}

blocks.caption: Further optimization: pure place value arithmetic, no array

codes.python:
def maximum69_number(num):
    place_value = 1
    temp = num
    while temp > 0:                 # find the largest place value present, no string built at all
        place_value *= 10
        temp //= 10
    place_value //= 10               # step back one, now it matches the leading digit's place
    while place_value > 0:
        digit = (num // place_value) % 10   # extract just this one digit, most significant first
        if digit == 6:
            return num + 3 * place_value     # 9 minus 6 is 3, this jumps straight to the flipped value
        place_value //= 10
    return num                                # no 6 found, the number is already maximal


if __name__ == "__main__":
    num = 9669
    print(maximum69_number(num))

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The first while loop exists purely to discover how many digits num has, expressed as its largest place value, without ever converting the number to a string.
Extracting a digit via (num / placeValue) % 10 pulls out exactly one digit at a time, most significant first, using only integer division and modulo.

Returning num + 3 * placeValue instead of rebuilding the whole number works because adding 3 times a 6's place value is mathematically identical to changing that one digit from 6 to 9, since 9 minus 6 equals 3.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(d), still a linear scan over the digit places.
Space: O(1) extra, since no digit array or string is ever built, a genuine improvement over the O(d) space used by the earlier two solutions.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

The core pattern here is recognizing that place value ordering decides greediness: whenever digits differ in significance, acting on the most significant one first is always at least as good as any other choice, so there is never a reason to explore further once that first opportunity is found. This same reasoning shows up constantly in digit and place value problems.
Common Mistakes

items: Flipping every 6 instead of just the leftmost one, which can produce a smaller number than necessary.
Forgetting that the change is optional, a number with no 6 at all should be returned unchanged.
Rebuilding the number incorrectly after editing a digit array, for example forgetting to convert characters back to integers.

blocks.text: Interview Tips

This problem is a good test of whether you reach for brute force first or spot the greedy shortcut immediately. Explaining why the leftmost digit dominates, rather than just stating it, is what separates a memorized answer from real understanding, and it is exactly the kind of reasoning interviewers want to hear out loud.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid trying every 6", think: scan left to right and stop at the first one, since place value ordering makes it always optimal.
If the interviewer says "can you do this with O(1) extra space", think: work directly with place value arithmetic, division and modulo, instead of a digit array or string.
If the interviewer says "what if more than one flip were allowed", think: the same place value ordering still applies, just flip the leftmost k sixes instead of only one.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Can you solve this without ever converting the number to a string or digit array?
What would change if up to k flips were allowed instead of just one?
What if the allowed flip were 9 to 6 instead of 6 to 9, minimizing instead of maximizing?
Can you prove why the leftmost 6 is always at least as good as any other choice, not just state it?
How would the approach change if the digits were not guaranteed to only be 6s and 9s?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Any problem where a single bounded edit, one swap, one flip, one increment, should be applied at the most significant position available, since place value ordering makes that always optimal.
Greedy digit manipulation problems in general, where trying every option is a safe brute force fallback but the leftmost, most significant choice usually dominates.
Place value arithmetic tricks, extracting digits with division and modulo, editing a digit via addition instead of rebuilding a string, that reappear in many math heavy interview problems.
Early termination, stopping the moment the provably optimal move is found, as a broader pattern for greedy algorithms in general.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(d squared) time. Both optimizations bring that down to O(d) time. The further optimization additionally drops space from O(d) down to O(1), by working directly with place value arithmetic instead of ever building a digit array.
13. Final Summary

items: Pattern: greedy choice driven by place value, the most significant available option always wins.
Core Idea: only the leftmost 6 ever needs to be flipped, since place value strictly decreases moving right and a flip always adds the same 3 times its place value.
Time: O(d squared) for the brute force, O(d) for both optimized versions.
Space: O(d) for the first two versions, O(1) for the further optimized place value arithmetic version.
Most Important Observation: this problem only looks like it needs trying every option; in reality exactly one digit, the leftmost 6, ever needs to be touched.
Interview Difficulty: easy on the surface, the real test is explaining why the leftmost digit dominates rather than just asserting it.
One line memory trick: leftmost 6 wins, always, stop the moment you find it.
